Aged Citrus Peel (Chenpi) Prevents
Acetaminophen-Induced Hepatotoxicity by
Epigenetically Regulating Nrf2 Pathway
Zi-Han Lin, * Yen-Fan Chan, * Min-Hsiung Pan, †,‡,§ Yen-Chen Tung † and
Zheng-Yuan Su *
*Department of Bioscience Technology
Chung Yuan Christian University
Taoyuan City , Taiwan
†Institute of Food Science and Technology
National Taiwan University
Taipei, Taiwan
‡Department of Medical Research
China Medical University Hospital
China Medical University
Taichung, Taiwan
§Department of Health and Nutrition Biotechnology
Asia University
Taichung, Taiwan
Published 4 December 2019
Abstract: Excessive consumption of analgesic drug acetaminophen (APAP) can cause severe
oxidative stress-mediated liver injury. Here, we investigated the protective effect and
mechanism of aged citrus peel (Chenpi, CP), a Chinese herb usually used in foods in Asia,
against APAP-induced hepatotoxicity. CP water (CP-WE), ethanolic (CP-EE), and water
extraction residue ethanolic (CP-WREE) extracts were prepared. We found that CP-WREE
contained higher content of bioactive ﬂavonoids, including narirutin, nobiletin, and tanger-
etin, and more effectively enhanced the Nrf2 pathway in ARE-luciferase reporter gene
transfected human HepG2-C8 cells. In mouse AML-12 hepatocytes, CP-WREE minimized
APAP-induced damage and lipid peroxidation and increased mRNA and protein expressions
of Nrf2 and its downstream defense enzymes (HO-1, NQO1, and UGT1A). CP-WREE also
downregulated HDACs and DNMTs, upregulated KDMs, and increased the unmethylated
Nrf2 promoter level. Additionally, CP-WREE blocked in vitro DNA methyltransferase

activity. Taken together, CP-WREE might attenuate oxidative stress-induced hepatotoxicity
through epigenetically regulating Nrf2-mediated cellular defense system.
Keywords: Acetaminophen; Aged Citrus Peel; Hepatotoxicity; Epigenetics; Liver; Nrf2.
Introduction
The liver is mainly responsible for the metabolism and biotransformation of various
substances, including proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, vitamins, hormones, bile, drugs, and
toxins. Common liver diseases include acute and chronic hepatitis, fatty liver, liver cir-
rhosis, and hepatic cancer, which can cause life-threatening metabolic disorders ( Kneeman
et al. , 2012). Acetaminophen ( N-acetyl-p-aminophenol, APAP), also known as paraceta-
mol, is a common antipyretic and analgesic drug; however, an overdose of APAP may
cause severe liver damage and failure ( James et al., 2003). In the liver, 55% of APAP can
be metabolized into water-soluble APAP-glucuronide and 30% into APAP-sulfate and then
excreted in bile or urine, whereas approximately 15% of APAP will be transferred by phase
I cytochrome P450 enzymes (CYPs) into a highly hepatotoxic metabolite N-acetyl-
p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI) ( Yoon et al. , 2016). A small amount of NAPQI can be
conjugated into hydrophilic APAP-glutathione by glutathione S-transferase (GST) and
ﬁnally metabolized into APAP-mercapturic acid, APAP-cysteine, or APAP- N-acetyl cys-
teine (NAC) for excretion ( Jaeschke and Bajt , 2006). However, when taking high doses of
APAP, accumulating NAPQI in the phase I pathway will deplete glutathione (GSH) and
rapidly increase reactive oxygen species in the liver, resulting in sever toxic damage
(Mazaleuskaya et al. , 2015).
Accumulating evidence shows that gene expression is strictly regulated by epigenetic
modiﬁcations, mainly including DNA methylation and histone modi ﬁcation. DNA
methyltransferases (DNMTs) catalyze the methylation of cytosine at position 5 in the CpG
dinucleotides in DNA, especially on CpG islands, which interferes the binding of RNA
polymerase to DNA and reduces transcription ( Lee et al. , 2013). The main DNMTs,
including DNMTs 1, 3A, and 3B, can transfer the methyl group from S-adenosyl methi-
onine (SAM) to cytosine ( Moore et al. , 2013). Post-translational modi ﬁcations of
histones alter the interaction between histones and DNA, which regulates gene expression
(Khorasanizadeh, 2004). The modi ﬁcation mainly occurs on speci ﬁc amino acids in the
histones, with modi ﬁcation including phosphorylation, acetylation, methylation, ubiquiti-
nation, SUMOylation, and ADP-ribosylation ( Bannister and Kouzarides , 2011). Acetyla-
tion can reduce the interaction between histones and DNA to activate transcription,
whereas lysine methylation at different positions in histones may inhibit or trigger tran-
scription ( Bannister and Kouzarides , 2011
). The enzymes responsible for histone modi ﬁ-
cation include histone deacetyltransferases (HDACs) and histone demethylases (KDMs)
(Black et al. , 2012). In recent years, some dietary phytochemicals have been discovered
to re-activate silenced genes by epigenetic regulation to prevent/treat human diseases
(Su et al. , 2013a, 2014; Guo et al. , 2015).

Nuclear factor erythroid-2-related factor-2 (NFE2L2 or Nrf2) is a transcription factor
responsible for regulating the expressions of some cellular anti-oxidant and detoxi ﬁcation
enzymes ( Huang et al. , 2015). Under normal condition, inactivated Nrf2 is degraded by
ubiquitin when a Kelch-like RCH-associated protein 1 (Keap1)-Nrf2-Cul3 complex forms in
the cytoplasm (Huang et al., 2015). When intracellular oxidative stress is generated, activated
Nrf2 leaving from the complex enters the nucleus and subsequently binds to the anti-oxidant
response elements (AREs) with small Maf, which triggers the transcription of downstream
anti-oxidant and detoxifying enzymes, including heme oxygenase 1 (HO-1), NAD(P)H:
quinone oxidoreductase-1 (NQO1), and UDP-glucuronosyltransferases (UGTs), to suppress
oxidant stress-induced cellular injuries (Su et al., 2013b). Therefore, Nrf2 also play a critical
role to prevent some oxidative stress caused liver diseases, such as drug-induced liver injury,
alcoholic liver injury, steatohepatitis, and cirrhosis ( Jadeja et al., 2016). Some dietary phy-
tochemicals, such as sulforaphane (SFN), ginsenoside Rb1, caffeic acid, curcumin, and
lycopene, have been demonstrated to activate the Nrf2 pathway and enhance intracellular
anti-oxidant capacity, which alleviates the diseases caused by oxidative stress ( Lee et al. ,
2013). Moreover, accumulating evidence shows the role of epigenetic modi ﬁcations in
regulating Nrf2 pathway by dietary phytochemicals ( Su et al., 2014; Cheng et al., 2016).
Aged citrus peel (Chenpi, CP) is made from the dried peel of orange or tangerine
belonging to the family Rutaceae and used as a Chinese traditional medicine and seasoning
in Asia. The citrus peel is mainly composed of essential oils, pectin, phenolic acid, ﬂa-
vonoids, and polymethoxy ﬂavonoids (PMFs) ( Gualdani et al. , 2016). Some studies have
reported that PMFs are the novel active compounds in citrus peel, as their various
bioactivities have continuously been demonstrated, including anticancer, antibacterial,
antidiabetic, and anti-oxidative effects ( Ernawita et al. , 2017). It has been demonstrated
that supplementation of Citrus maxima peel powder can alleviate carbon tetrachloride
(CCl
4)-induced liver injury in rats ( Chowdhury et al. , 2015). Therefore, this suggests that
CP might have hepatoprotective potential. However, studies on the protective effect and
mechanism for CP against APAP-induced hepatotoxicity are still scarce. In the present
study, we investigated hepatoprotective activity of CP extracts against APAP-induced
oxidative stress in normal mouse AML-12 hepatocytes through Nrf2 pathway and epige-
netic mechanisms.
Materials and Methods
Chemicals
Ethanol (95% and 99.8%) was purchased from Echo Chemical (Miaoli, Taiwan).
D,L-sulforaphane (SFN) was from Toronto Research Chemicals (North York, ON,
Canada). Methanol, dimethyl sulfoxide, acetaminophen (APAP), quercetin, and dexa-
methasone were supplied by Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, MO, USA). Fetal bovine serum
(FBS), penicillin-streptomycin, trypsin-EDTA, Dulbecco ’s modi ﬁed eagle medium
(DMEM), and Dulbecco ’s modi ﬁed eagle medium/nutrient mixture F-12 (DMEM/F-12)
were gained by Gibco (Grand Island, NY, USA). Insulin-transferrin-selenium mixture was

purchased from GeneDireX (Las Vegas city, NV, USA). All antibodies were obtained
from GeneTex (Irvine, CA, USA), including Nrf2, HO-1, NQO1, UGT1A, DNMT1,
DNMT3A, HDAC1, HDAC2, HDAC8, HDAC4/5/9, JMJD3, UTX/KDM6A, and β-actin
antibodies. Enzymes M.SssI and BstUI were from New England Biolabs (Ipswich,
MA, USA).
Preparation of Sample
CP was purchased from local market and ground into powder and then 100 g of CP powder
was cooked with 2 L of boiling ddH 2O for 5 min to obtain water extract (CP-WE).
One gram of CP powder and the CP residue after water extraction were stirred in 40 mL of
95% ethanol at 200 rpm at 25 /C14 C for 24 h to obtain ethanolic extract (CP-EE) and water
extraction residue ethanolic extract (CP-WREE), respectively. CP-WE, CP-EE, and CP-
WREE were ﬁltered and then vaporized to dryness under vacuum, and their yields were
57.08, 44.32, and 8.71 g/100 g dry weight (DW), respectively.
Flavonoids Analysis
PMFs in the extracts were analyzed by using reversed-phase high performance liquid
chromatography (RP-HPLC) according to the reported method with slightly modi ﬁcation
(Lu et al. , 2013). Brie ﬂy, the extracts were dissolved in methanol at 20 mg/mL and then
ﬁltered with 0.45 μm membrane. The contents of 2 PMFs (nobiletin and tangeretin), a
methoxyﬂavone glycoside (hesperidin), and a ﬂavanone glycoside (narirutin) were deter-
mined at 280 nm by using a liquid chromatography system (Agilent Technologies, Santa
Clara, CA, USA) equipped with a C18 Column ( 250 /C2 4:6 mm, 5 μm) (Agilent Technol-
ogies, Santa Clara, CA, USA). The injection volume of sample was 10 μL and the column
was operated at 30 /C14 C.
Total Phenolic Content
The total phenolic content of the extracts was determined by the Folin-Ciocalteu colorimetric
method modiﬁed from the reported study ( Ainsworth and Gillespie, 2007). Brieﬂy, 50 μLo f
the extracts or gallic acid as a standard dissolved in 95% methanol were mixed thoroughly
with 100 μL of 10% Folin & Ciocalteu’s phenol reagent, followed by the addition of 400μLo f
700 mM sodium carbonate. After 60 min of incubation at 25/C14 C, the absorbance of the reaction
mixture was measured at 650 nm using a microplate spectrophotometer (Beckman, Brea, CA,
USA). The total phenolic content was calculated from the calibration curve, and the results
were expressed as mg gallic acid equivalent (GAE) per 100 g DW.
Total Flavonoids Content
The total ﬂavonoid content of the extracts was determined by the aluminum chloride
colorimetric method modi ﬁed from the reported study ( Chang et al., 2002). Brieﬂy, 50 μL

sium acetate, and 500 μL of ddH 2O. After 30 min of incubation at 25 /C14 C, the absorbance of
the reaction mixture was measured at 415 nm using a microplate spectrophotometer
(Beckman, Brea, CA, USA). The total phenolic content was calculated from the calibration
curve, and the results were expressed as mg quercetin equivalent (QE) per 100 g DW.
Cell Culture and Treatment
Human hepatoma HepG2-C8 cells stably transfected with a pARE-TI-luciferase reporter
gene were provided by Dr. Ah-Ng Tony Kong (Rutgers University, New Brunswick, NJ,
USA) (Su et al., 2013a). HepG2-C8 cells were maintained in DMEM containing 10% FBS
and 1% penicillin-streptomycin solution. Murine hepatocyte derived AML12 cells (ATCC
CRL-2254) were maintained in DMEM/F-12 medium containing 10% FBS, 1% penicillin-
streptomycin solution, 40 ng/mL dexamethasone, 5.0 g/L insulin, 2.75 g/L transferrin, and
3.35 mg/L sodium selenite. The cells were cultured at 37 /C14 C in a humidi ﬁed incubator with
5% CO 2 atmosphere. When treating HepG2-C8 or AML12 cells, cells were seeded in the
medium containing 10% FBS for 24 h and then cultured in a new medium containing 1%
FBS with or without treatments for another period.
Assay for Cell Viability
After being cultured in 96-well plates for 24 h, HepG2-C8 ( 1:0 /C2 104 cells/100 μL/well)
and AML-12 ( 5:0 /C2 103 cells/100 μL/well) cells were treated with various extracts for
another 24 h and 72 h, respectively, for a cytotoxicity test. In addition, to evaluate the effect
of CP-WREE on APAP-induced cell damage, AML-12 cells ( 5:0 /C2 103 cells/100 μL/well)
were seeded in 96-well plates for 24 h and then pre-treated with various extracts for an
additional 24 h. The cells were further co-treated with various extracts and APAP (3.6 mM)
for 48 h. The cells were subjected to CellTiter 96 AQueous One Solution (MTS) Cell
Proliferation Assay (Promega, Madison, WI, USA). Cell viability was determined by
measuring the absorbance at 490 nm using a microplate spectrophotometer (Beckman,
Brea, CA, USA).
ARE-Luciferase Reporter Activity Assay
After HepG2-C8 ( 1:0 /C2 105 cells/mL/well) cells were seeded in 12-well plates for 24 h, the
cells were treated with different concentrations of extracts for another 24 h. Luciferase
activity was determined using a luciferase detection kit (Promega, Madison, WI, USA) as
described previously (Su et al., 2013a). The cells were washed twice with ice-cold PBS and
then stored in 1X reporter lysis buffer at /C0 20
/C14 C overnight. The supernatant of cell lysate
was analyzed using a microplate spectrophotometer (Beckman, Brea, CA, USA). Protein
concentration was determined by bicinchoninic acid (BCA) assay (G-Biosciences, St.
Louis, MO, USA) to normalize the luciferase activity.

Measurement of Thiobarbituric Acid-Reactive Substances (TBARS)
The level of malondialdehyde (MDA), a product of lipid peroxidation, was measured by
using OXI-TEK TBARS assay kit (Enzo Life Sciences, Farmingdale, NY, USA). Brie ﬂy,
AML-12 cells ( 5:0 /C2 105 cells/10 mL/10-cm dish) were pre-treated with CP-WREE for
24 h and then co-incubated with CP-WREE and 3.6 mM APAP for another 48 h. The cells
were scraped in 1X PBS containing 1% Triton X-100. The supernatant of cell lysate mixed
with 20 μL of SDS solution and 500 μL of thiobarbituric acid (TBA)/buffer reagent was
incubated at 95 /C14 C for 60 min and then cooled in an ice bath for 10 min. The reactive
products were centrifuged and the supernatant was removed for analysis using a ﬂuores-
cence spectrophotometer (Beckman, Brea, CA, USA) with excitation at 488 nm and
emission at 530 nm. The TBARS results were expressed in nmole MDA per mg protein.
RNA Isolation and Quantitative Real-Time PCR (qPCR)
AML-12 cells ( 5:0 /C2 10
5 cells/10 mL/10 cm dish) were washed twice with ice-cold PBS
and then harvested after the treatment with CP-WREE for 72 h. RNA was extracted using
total RNA isolation kit (GeneDireX, Las Vegas City, NV, USA). First strand cDNA
synthesized from total RNA using iScript cDNA synthesis kit (Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA,
USA) was used as the template for the determination of mRNA expression by qPCR with
iQ SYBR Green Supermix (Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA, USA) in a real-time PCR detection
system (Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA, USA). The following primers were used: β-actin (sense
50-CGT TCA ATA CCC CAG CCA TG-3 0 and antisense 5 0-GAC CCC GTC ACC AGA
GTC C-3 0), Nrf2 (sense 5 0-AGC AGG ACT GGA GAA GTT-3 0 and antisense 5 0-TTC
TTT TTC CAG CGA GGA GA-3 0), HO-1 (sense 5 0-CCT CAC TGG CAG GAA ATC
ATC-30 and antisense 5 0-CCT CGT GGA GAC GCT TTA CAT A-3 0), NQO1 (sense 5 0-
AGC CCA GAT ATT GTG GCC G-3 0 and antisense 5 0-CCT TTC AGA ATG GCT GGC
AC-30), and UGT1A1 (sense 5 0-GAA ATT GCT GAG GCT TTG GGC AGA-3 0 and
antisense 5 0-ATG GGA GCC AGA GTG TGT GAT GAA-3 0)( Su et al. , 2013a).
Western Blotting
AML-12 cells ( 5:0 /C2 105 cells/10 mL/10-cm dish) treated with CP-WREE for 72 h were
washed twice with ice-cold PBS and then harvested in lysis buffer (Promega, Madison,
WI, USA) at /C0 20/C14 C overnight. The samples (25 μg of total protein) were loaded onto a
SDS-polyacrylamide gel to run gel electrophoresis. Proteins were transferred onto a
polyvinylidene di ﬂuoride membrane (Millipore, Burlington, MA, USA) using a semidry
transfer system (Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA, USA). After hybridization with primary antibody,
the immunoreactions were continued with horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-conjugated sec-
ondary antibodies. The immunoblots on the membranes were determined by Immobilon
western chemiluminescent HRP substrate (Millipore, Burlington, MA, USA) using Lu-
minescent Image Analyzer (Fuji ﬁlm, Tokyo, Japan). The intensity of bands was quanti ﬁed
by densitometry using Image J [Version 1.80, National Institutes of Health (NIH)].

DNA Extraction and Methylation Speci ﬁc PCR (MSP)
AML-12 cells (5:0 /C2 105 cells/10 mL/10-cm dish) were washed twice with ice-cold PBS and
then harvested after the treatment with CP-WREE for 72 h. DNA was extracted from the cells
with a genomic DNA (gDNA) isolation kit (GeneDireX, Las Vegas City, NV, USA), and
bisulﬁte conversion of the gDNA was performed with an EZ DNA Methylation-Lightning kit
(Zymo Research, Irvine, CA, USA) following the manufacturer’s instructions. The fragment
of murine Nrf2 promoter which contains CpG islands located between /C0 1226 and /C0 1086
relative to the initiation codon in converted gDNA was quanti ﬁed using qPCR ( Su et al. ,
2013a). Next, bisulﬁte converted gDNA was subjected to perform PCR by ZymoTaq PreMix
kit (Zymo Research, Irvine, CA, USA). The ampliﬁed products were separated by 2% agarose
gel electrophoresis and then photographed by gel documentation system (VILBER, Collé-
gien, France). The intensity of bands were quantiﬁed by densitometry using Image J (Version
1.80, NIH). The following primers were used: bisul ﬁte-modiﬁed Nrf2 promoter (sense 5 0-
TTG AGA GGT GGG GTT TTA-3 0 and antisense 5 0-ACC AAC TAC CCT CTA ACC-3 0),
methylated Nrf2 promoters (sense 50-TAA TAT GAA TTA TAT TAA AGG GTT GT-30 and
antisense 5 0-CCT AAA CTC AAA ACC CAA ACA AT-3 0), and unmethylated Nrf2 pro-
moters (sense 5 0-TAA TAC GAA TTA TAT TAA AGG GTC GT-3 0 and antisense 5 0-CTA
AAC TCG AAA CCC AAA CGA T-3 0).
In Vitro Methylation Assay
This assay was adapted from a previous study ( Su et al. , 2013a). The region of the
human p16 Ink4a gene between position /C0 444 and 401 relative to the initiation codon was
ampliﬁed as the substrate DNA by ZymoTaq PreMix kit (Zymo Research, Irvine, CA,
USA). The primers for amplifying the p16 Ink4a DNA fragment were as follows: sense 5 0-
G G CT C CT C CG C AT T CT C - 30 and antisense 5 0-CTC GTC GAA AGT CTT CCA
TTC T-3 0.T h ea m p l iﬁed products separated by 2% agarose gel electrophoresis were
extracted by PCR clean-up and a gel extraction kit (GeneDireX, Las Vegas City, NV,
USA) following the manufacturer ’s instructions. Next, the substrate DNA was mixed
with various concentrations of CP-WREE, 1600 μM S-adenosyl methionine (SAM), and
4 units of M.SssI (a CpG methylase) in 1X NEB buffer at 37 /C14 C for 1 h. Then 30 units of
BstUI (a restriction enzyme) was added into the reaction mixture to digest the unme-
thylated sites in the substrate DNA at 60 /C14 C for another 1 h. The methylated DNA (larger
fragments) and unmethylated DNA (smeared fragments of < 850 bp) bands were ana-
lyzed by 2% agarose gel electrophoresis and gel documentation system (VILBER,
Collégien, France). The intensity of bands was quanti ﬁed by densitometry using Image J
(Version 1.80, NIH).
Statistical Analysis
The data are represented as means /C6 SD (standard deviation) from three independent
experiments. One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Duncan ’s multiple comparison

Results
The Content of Flavonoid and Total Phenolics in CP Extracts
The contents of four bioactive ﬂavonoids, total phenolic, and total ﬂavonoids in CP-WE,
CP-EE, and CP-WREE are shown in Table 1. RP-HPLC was performed to analyze the
contents of hesperidin (5,7,3 0-trihydroxy-40-methoxyﬂavone-7-O-rutinoside), narirutin
(40,5,7-trihydroxyﬂavanone-7-O-rutinoside), nobiletin (3 0,40,5,6,7,8-hexamethoxyﬂavone),
and tangeretin (4 0,5,6,7,8-pentamethoxyﬂavone). CP-WE contained the highest amount of
hesperidin (12.62 mg/g DW), followed by CP-WREE (9.98 mg/g DW) and CP-EE
(3.71 mg/g DW). However, CP-WREE showed the highest level of narirutin (6.08 mg/g
DW), nobiletin (2.78 mg/g DW), and tangeretin (2.88 mg/g DW) among three extracts,
while the contents of nobiletin and tangeretin in CP-WE were not detectable. Total phe-
nolic and ﬂavonoid contents of CP-WREE were 18.11 mg GAE and 10.55 mg QE per gram
dry weight, respectively, which were also higher than the content of CP-WE and CP-EE.
These results indicate that CP-WREE is a phenolic, ﬂavonoids, and PMF-rich extract.
CP-WREE Induces ARE-Luciferase Reporter Activity in Human HepG2-C8 Cells
We used HepG2-C8 cells stably transfected with the ARE-luciferase reporter vector to
evaluate the effect of the CP extracts with hepatoprotective potential on Nrf2-ARE acti-
vation. First, the results showed that all treatments of CP-WE, CP-EE, and CP-WREE (0 –
100 μg/mL) did not have signi ﬁcant cytotoxicity in HepG2-C8 cells after being treated with
the extracts for 24 h (Fig. 1A). CP-WREE at 100 μg/mL signi ﬁcantly induced relative
luciferase activity ( 2:2 /C6 0:6 fold) in HepG2-C8 cells compared to that in the control

CP-WREE Attenuates APAP-Induced Injury and Oxidative Stress in Mouse
AML-12 Hepatocytes
The protective effect and mechanism of CP against APAP-induced hepatotoxicity still
remain unclear. Before using animal models to elucidate the ef ﬁcacy and safety of CP,
mouse AML-12 cells derived from CD1 mouse hepatocytes were preferred to evaluate the
hepatoprotective potential of various CP extracts ( Ahmed et al., 2011, 2016). In this study,
since we found that CP-WREE treatment had showed the best ARE activity induction, we
further evaluated the hepatoprotective effect of various CP extracts in AML-12 cells. As
shown in Fig. 2A, CP-WE, CP-EE, and CP-WREE (0 –50 μg/mL) did not exhibit a toxic
effect against AML-12 cells after 72 h of treatment ( p < 0:05).
Therefore, we evaluated the protective potential of various extracts (0 –50 μg/mL)
against APAP-induced AML-12 cell damage. AML-12 hepatocytes were pre-incubated
with various extracts for 24 h and then co-treated with various extracts and APAP (3.6 mM)
for an additional 48 h. As shown in Fig. 2B, APAP signi ﬁcantly decreased AML-12 cell
viability compared to that in the control treatment after 48 h of treatment ( p < 0:05),
whereas only CP-WREE at 25 and 50 μg/mL signiﬁcantly reversed the cell death caused by

CP-WREE Regulates the Expressions of Epigenetic Modifying Enzymes
in Mouse AML-12 Hepatocytes
The hepatoprotective activity of CP-WREE by triggering Nrf2 mediated oxidative stress
response pathway has been demonstrated in AML-12 cells. We further investigated the
epigenetic mechanism for CP-WREE on histone deacetylases, DNA methyltransferases,
and histone demethylases (JMJD3 and UTX/KDM6A). We found that CP-WREE at 25 and
50 μg/mL signiﬁcantly decreased the protein expression of HDAC8 in AML-12 cells after
3 days of treatment ( p < 0:05, Fig. 5A). CP-WREE repressed the expression of the
HDACs 1, 2, and 4/5/9 proteins, but no signi ﬁcant difference was observed. Conversely,
CP-WREE signi ﬁcantly enhanced the protein expression of JMJD3 and UTX/KDM6A
(p < 0:05, Fig. 5A). Consistent with the DNMTs expression, CP-WREE at 25 and 50 μg/
mL signi ﬁcantly decreased the protein levels of DNMT1 ( p < 0:05 and p < 0:001, re-
spectively, Fig. 5B). Protein expression of DNMT3A was also signi ﬁcantly suppressed by
CP-WREE at 25 and 50 μg/mL ( p < 0:05). These results suggest that epigenetic
mechanisms may be important for CP-WREE to activate Nrf2 gene transcription, espe-
cially alternating DNA methylation.
CP-WREE Demethylates Nrf2 Promoter in Mouse AML-12 Hepatocytes and Inhibits
DNMT Activity In Vitro
DNA methylation is one of the critical epigenetic mechanisms for controlling gene ex-
pression in eukaryotes. We have found that CP-WREE decreased the protein expressions of
DNMTs 1 and 3A which are the important enzymes to transfer and maintain methyl-CpG
sites in DNA in AML-12 cells. We further performed Methylation Speci ﬁc PCR (MSP)
assays to con ﬁrm whether CP-WREE demethylated the Nrf2 promoter by which CP-
WREE triggered Nrf2 mRNA expression. After the quantitation by qPCR, the same
amount of bisul ﬁte Nrf2 promoter fragment between /C0 1226 and /C0 1086 relative to the
initiation codon was subjected to MSP assay. CP-WREE (25 μg/mL) signi ﬁcantly in-
creased the level of unmethylated Nrf2 promoter ( p < 0:05, Fig. 6A), while the level of
methylated Nrf2 promoter expression was slightly decreased (Fig. 6A without the quan-
titative results). Furthermore, in order to examine the inhibitory effect of CP-WREE on
DNMT activity, we used a human p16 Ink4a gene PCR product (850 bp) as a substrate DNA
and the puriﬁed recombinant CpG methyltransferase (M.SssI) containing a similar structure
to the DNMT1 catalytic domain. A restriction enzyme BstUI digested the unmethylated
DNA which was not incubated with M.SssI into smaller fragments (Fig. 6B). CP-WREE
signiﬁcantly inhibited CpG methyltransferase activity in a dose-dependent manner from 50
to 1000 μg/mL ( p < 0:05). These results indicate that CP-WREE can drive the transcrip-
tional activation of Nrf2 by blocking DNMT activity to reverse the DNA methylation
status of Nrf2 gene promoter.

Discussion
Many studies demonstrate that the activation of Nrf2-mediated detoxi ﬁcation/anti-oxidant
pathway ameliorates oxidative stress-induced hepatic injury ( Tang et al., 2014). It has also
reported that dietary phytochemicals can effectively activate the Nrf2 anti-oxidant pathway
in the hepatocytes, which increases Nrf2 downstream anti-oxidant and detoxifying
enzymes to suppress the oxidative stress induced by drugs, chemicals, alcohol, nonalco-
holic steatohepatitis, and cholestasis ( Jadeja et al. , 2016). For example, sulforaphane
(SFN) obtained from cruciferous vegetables protects the mice from acetaminophen
(APAP)-induced liver injury through the activation of Nrf2 pathway ( Noh et al. , 2015).
Additionally, most phenolic compounds and ﬂavonoids have free radical scavenging
ability due to their redox properties, contributing to the anti-oxidant activity, and some of

them also exhibit Nrf2 pathway induction activity in many studies ( Huang et al. , 2015).
PMFs (such as nobiletin and tangeretin) and ﬂavone glycosides (such as hesperidin and
narirutin) are ﬂavonoid compounds in citrus peel also show anti-oxidative effects, in-
cluding cellular Nrf2 pathway induction ( Ernawita et al. , 2017). In this study, we found
that CP-WREE contains higher narirutin, nobiletin, and tangeretin contents when compared
to the other two extracts, CP-WE and CP-EE (Table 1). In addition, CP-WREE also had
higher amounts of total phenolic and ﬂavonoid compounds, followed by CP-EE and CP-
WE (Table 1). It has been known that activated Nrf2 must bind to the anti-oxidant response
elements (AREs) for triggering the transcriptional activation of many detoxifying and anti-
oxidant enzymes ( Huang et al., 2015). We also found CP-WREE induced ARE-luciferase
activity as much as SFN in HepG2-C8 cells, but not CP-WE and CP-EE (Figs. 1B
and 1C), while CP-WREE did not affect cell viability (Fig. 1A). Therefore, CP-WREE is a
candidate with hepatoprotective potential against oxidative stress-induced liver damage.
APAP is one of the most commonly used components in analgesics around the world;
however, it has been known for decades that long-term and high-dose APAP consumption
may result in liver injury and subsequent liver failure ( Yoon et al. , 2016). The maximum
recommended dose of APAP for usual therapy is 4.0 g in adults and 50 –75 mg/kg in
children per day ( Mazaleuskaya et al. , 2015). A highly reactive N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone
imine (NAPQI) intermediate (5 –10%) formed from APAP oxidation catalyzed by phase I
CYPs in the liver ( Yoon et al. , 2016). NAPQI can further be scavenged when conjugated
with GSH, but excessive APAP can induce oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction
after the depletion of GSH, resulting in hepatic injury ( James et al., 2003). In Mouse AML-
12 hepatocytes, it has been demonstrated that the treatment of APAP (10 mM) for 24 h
caused a signi ﬁcant increase in reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and GSH de-
pletion ( Ahmed et al. , 2016). AML-12 hepatocytes were used for elucidating the role of
Nrf2 and an important enzyme AKR7A responsible for biodetoxi ﬁcation against APAP/
NAPQI-induced oxidative stress and hepatotoxicity, and a similar effect was also obtained
in an in vivo study using Sprague-Dawley rats ( Ahmed et al., 2011). In our study, APAP at
3.6 mM displays a signi ﬁcant hepatotoxic effect in mouse AML-12 cells after 48 h treat-
ment, including decreased cell viability and increased cell shrinking and ﬂoating, com-
plicated by a signi ﬁcant increase of oxidative stress (Figs. 2B and 3). Excitingly, we found
that CP-WREE without cytotoxicity signi ﬁcantly exhibits protective activity
against APAP-induced hepatotoxicity and lipid peroxidation in mouse AML-12 cells
(Figs. 2 and 3).
The phase II metabolic enzymes are able to catalyze the anti-oxidant and detoxifying
reactions to not only reduce the toxicity of intermediates from the phase I metabolism but
also to reduce intracellular oxidative stress in hepatocytes, contributing to hepatoprotection
(Huang et al. , 2015). The phase II anti-oxidant and detoxifying enzymes include HO-1,
NQO1, UGTs, etc., and Nrf2 is a major regulator for controlling the transcriptional acti-
vation of these enzymes ( Tang et al., 2014). It has been demonstrated that the treatments of
some phytochemicals, such as SFN and caffeic acid, is a good strategy to reduce APAP-
induced hepatic injury by promoting Nrf2-mediated transcriptional activation of these
phase II enzymes ( Noh et al. , 2015; Pang et al. , 2016). A PMF-enriched citrus extract

exhibits preventive activity against non-alcoholic fatty liver disease in mice via the acti-
vation of Nrf2 pathway ( Ke et al. , 2018). Three methoxy ﬂavones (hesperidin, nobiletin,
and tangeretin) and narirutin can activate the Nrf2/ARE pathway to suppress various
oxidative stress-mediated liver injuries ( Mahmoud et al. , 2017; Hernandez-Aquino and
Muriel, 2018; Liang et al. , 2018). Our study showed that CP-WREE treatment effectively
blocks oxidative stress-induced hepatotoxicity in AML-12 cells caused by APAP via in-
ducing mRNA and protein expressions of Nrf2 and Nrf2 downstream enzymes including
HO-1, NQO1, and UGT1A (Fig. 4). Therefore, it is worthwhile clarifying how CP-WREE
increases the accumulation of cytoplasmic Nrf2.
In the recent years, phytochemicals can epigenetically reactivate the expression of Nrf2
pathway by regulating histone modi ﬁcation and DNA methylation ( Su et al., 2013a, 2014).
In this study, the results show that CP-WREE induces a signi ﬁcant increased HDAC8
protein level and a slight increase of HDACs 1, 2, and 4/5/9 protein levels in AML-12 cells
(Fig. 5A). The promoters in chromatin enriched in trimethylated histone 3 at lysine 27
(H3K27me3) are inactive since DNA is tightly packed ( Black et al. , 2012). Histone
demethylases, such as JMJD3 and UTX/KDM6A, are responsible for the demethylation of
H3K27me3, resulting in the re-expression of some silencing genes ( Hong et al., 2007). Our
study indicates that CP-WREE induced slight and signi ﬁcant expressions of JMJD3 and
UTX/KDM6A proteins in AML-12 cells, respectively (Fig. 5A). These results suggest that
CP-WREE may re-activate the Nrf2 pathway in AML-12 cells by regulating the expres-
sions of histone modifying enzymes, including HDACs and KDMs.
DNA demethylation is one of the strategies for many phytochemicals to restore Nrf2
gene expression ( Su et al. , 2013b). In mammalian cells, DNMT1 maintains DNA meth-
ylation during replication, whereas DNMT3A methylates the unmodi ﬁed DNA, which
results in gene silencing ( Moore et al. , 2013). We ﬁnd that CP-WREE signi ﬁcantly
decreases the protein levels of DNMTs 1 and 3A (Fig. 5B). Therefore, we presumed that
CP-WREE may induce the reactivation of Nrf2 gene expression by inducing demethylation
of the Nrf2 promoter region in AML-12 cells. We further demonstrated that CP-WREE
increases the levels of unmethylated Nrf2 promoters based on the result of methylation-
speciﬁc PCR (MSP) (Fig. 6A). Some phytochemicals inhibit the methylation of the Nrf2
gene promoter also by interfering with the activity of DNMTs ( Su et al. , 2013a, 2014).
Interestingly, it shows that CP-WREE in vitro blocks the activity of M.SssI, a recombinant
CpG methylase, in a dose-dependent manner (Fig. 6B). As has been frequently observed in
previous studies, such in vitro inhibition required a much larger dose than that in a cell
treatment model ( Khor et al. , 2011; Su et al. , 2013a). Taken together, in addition to
the decrease of DNMTs 1 and 3A proteins, it suggests that CP-WREE may also inhibit
the transfer of a methyl group from S-adenosyl methionine (SAM) to the cytosine in CpG
sites within Nrf2 promoters in AML-12 cells, resulting in mRNA re-expression of
Nrf2 gene.
In the present study, we found that CP-WREE shows the strongest induction effect on
Nrf2/ARE-luciferase activity in HepG2-C8 cells, which may be due to higher amount of
hesperidin, narirutin, nobiletin, and tangeretin in CP-WREE compared with CP-WE and
CP-EE. As shown in Fig. 7, CP-WREE may show its hepatoprotective effect by

UGT1A) in mouse AML-12 hepatocytes, contributing to its protective effect on oxidative
